# Diagnosing Rapid Brake Pad Wear After an Impact Event

If you are experiencing brake pads wearing out in a single wheel within a month or two of replacement, especially following a curb impact, the issue is almost certainly mechanical binding rather than normal friction wear. In your specific scenario with the 2007 Pontiac G6, the sequence of events points to a structural compromise that was likely missed during the initial repair at Firestone.

When a vehicle strikes a curb sideways, the energy transfer can cause subtle deformation in suspension components or steering knuckles that are not immediately visible as "bends" to an untrained eye. While bent rims and tires are obvious, internal misalignment of the control arms or the strut mounting points creates a geometry problem that persists long after the visual damage is fixed. If the wheel assembly is no longer perfectly perpendicular to the direction of travel, the brake caliper slides unevenly across the rotor surface. Instead of engaging symmetrically with both pads, one pad may drag while the other remains stationary, generating excessive heat and friction that shreds the friction material rapidly.

The fact that you replaced the rotor, caliper, and pads three times in quick succession suggests that the root causeâthe misalignmentâwas never addressed. A new rotor does not fix a bent suspension bushing or a distorted strut tower. Before ordering another set of pads, you need to verify the physical alignment of the wheel hub relative to the steering axis.

A definitive test involves checking for lateral play and binding at the caliper slide pins. Remove the brake assembly and inspect the piston seal and the guide pins. Even if the caliper slides freely by hand, internal corrosion or a damaged dust boot can cause the piston to stick slightly when reinstalled. This slight resistance prevents the caliper from retracting fully after braking, leading to constant drag on one side of the rotor.

However, given the history of curb impact, the most probable culprit is the suspension geometry. You may need to replace the lower control arm bushings or inspect the strut mount for damage. If the mounting point on the strut tower was compromised by the impact, the entire wheel assembly sits at an angle relative to the brake disc. This creates a constant drag force that standard brake pads cannot withstand without failing quickly.

Consider taking the vehicle to a shop that specializes in chassis alignment and suspension reconstruction rather than just wheel balancing. They can perform a three-ball alignment or use a specialized jig to check for side-to-side play in the strut assembly. If the strut itself is bent internally, no amount of pad replacement will fix the issue. The trade-off here is cost versus safety; driving with a dragging brake generates enough heat to warp new rotors and eventually cause brake fluid boil if the system gets hot enough under heavy load.

If you have confirmed that the suspension components are straight and the caliper slides smoothly, but the wear persists, investigate the parking brake cable adjustment on that specific wheel. A seized or misadjusted parking brake cable can prevent the rear brake shoes (if drum-in-hat) or the parking portion of the pads from releasing fully. However, based on the description of hitting a curb and the subsequent grind noise, suspension misalignment remains the primary suspect.

Until this mechanical binding is resolved, replacing parts will only be a temporary fix. The physics of the impact event likely introduced a permanent geometric distortion that requires component replacement or professional realignment to correct.
